text: According to the "National Report on caste/ethnicity, language & religion" from the National Population and Housing Census 2021, Nepal has 124 mother tongues. Of these, Nepali is the mother tongue for 44.86% of the population and serves as a second language for 46.2% of the total population. The languages of Nepal, referred to as Nepali languages in the country's constitution, are defined as those spoken by Nepalis with an ancient history or origin within Nepal's sovereign territory. These languages belong primarily to the Indo-Aryan and Sino-Tibetan language families, with only a few belonging to Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian families. The Indo-European family, specifically the Indo-Aryan (Indic) sub-family (excluding English), comprises 48 languages and accounts for nearly 82.1% of the population, including Nepali, Bhojpuri, Maithili, Awadhi, the Tharu languages, and Hindustani (Hindi-Urdu). The Sino-Tibetan family, part of the Tibeto-Burman group, includes about 63 languages and is spoken by 17.3% of the population, such as Tamang, Nepal Bhasa (Newar), Magar, and Limbu. The Dravidian family is represented by Kurux, and the Austro-Asiatic family by Santali and Mundari. Indigenous languages that predated the arrival of Indic, Tibeto-Burman, and other language families are nearly extinct, with only the Kusunda language surviving, though it is in a critical state. Nepal also has several indigenous village sign languages—Jhankot Sign Language, Jumla Sign Language, and Ghandruk Sign Language—as well as Nepali Sign Language for national use. The Constitution of Nepal 2015 (2072 B.S.) recognizes that all mother tongues spoken in Nepal are national languages. The Language Commission of Nepal in 2021 recommended 14 official languages for different provinces, with Nepali serving as the official working language at the federal level, while provinces are allowed to choose one or more additional official languages. Specific recommendations include Maithili and Limbu for Province No. 1; Maithili, Bhojpuri, and Bajjika for Province No. 2; Tamang and Nepal Bhasa for Bagmati Province; Magar and Gurung for Gandaki Province; Tharu and Awadhi for Lumbini Province; Nepali (Khas Bhasa) Karnali dialect and Magar for Karnali Province; Dotyali and Tharu for Sudurpashchim Province. Out of the 124 mother tongues, 111 were reported in the 2011 census, with 13 newly identified in 2021, including Bhote, Lowa, Chum/Nubri, Baragunwa, Nar-Phu, Ranatharu, Karmarong, Mugali, Tichhurong Poike, Sadri, Done, Munda/Mudiyari, and Kewarat. Some foreign languages from the 2011 census were included in the "Other Language" category due to very few speakers. In the 2021 census, 25 languages were used as a second language by more than 10,000 people each, compared to only 18 in the 2011 census. Most of Nepal's languages are found exclusively in oral form, and the Language Commission has identified fifteen scripts currently in use in the country.
